title: Galaxies' El Dorado
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1483, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1483 · about 40 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 1483 has a bright central bulge and hazy arms marked by distinct patches of star formation, while many more distant galaxies scatter the background. Hubble's view shows a barred spiral galaxy, which the source places in the southern constellation Dorado, a name meaning dolphinfish in Spanish.

Dorado hosts the Dorado Group, a loose gathering of an estimated 70 galaxies some 62 million light-years away. It is far bigger than the Local Group, the Milky Way's own group of around 30 galaxies, and comes close to the size of a galaxy cluster. Clusters are the largest structures in the Universe held together by gravity.

Barred spirals take their name from the bar-shaped structure across their centers. They make up about two thirds of all spiral galaxies, the Milky Way included. Recent studies suggest a bar may be a common stage in how spirals form, and possibly a sign that a galaxy has reached full maturity.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.39 x 1.46 arcminutes) and distance (40 million light years), the frame spans roughly 28,000 × 17,000 light-years. Its light set out about 40 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1483 in blue visible light at 435 nm and near-infrared light at 814 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, revealing many distant background galaxies.
